summary: Ardashir I overthrew the Parthians in 224 and his son Shapur I humiliated Rome, capturing the emperor Valerian in 260. For four centuries the Sasanians rivalled Rome and Byzantium; Khosrow I (531–579) sacked Antioch and took Yemen, and Khosrow II briefly held the Levant and Egypt. Exhausted by the war of 602–628 and the civil war that followed, the empire fell to the Arab conquests, ending with Yazdegerd III's death in 651.

details: In the early 3rd century the Parthian Empire was weakened by a long struggle between the brothers Vologases VI and Artabanus IV. Meanwhile Ardashir, a prince of the Sasanian family in Pars (Persis, south-western Iran), was conquering neighbouring provinces such as Kirman. On 28 April 224 Artabanus finally marched against him and was defeated and killed on the plain of Hormozdgan, whose exact site has never been found. The battle ended almost five centuries of Parthian rule, and Ardashir took the title 'King of Kings', founding a new Persian empire that soon held the Iranian plateau and Mesopotamia.

Shapur I, Ardashir's son, repeatedly invaded Rome's eastern provinces and plundered Antioch in 253 or 256. The ageing emperor Valerian marched east to stop him, and in 260 the two armies met between Carrhae and Edessa (modern Urfa, in Turkey). The Romans were defeated and besieged, and when Valerian tried to negotiate he was captured: the first Roman emperor ever taken prisoner. He died in Persian captivity, while Shapur's troops raided Cilicia and Cappadocia and deported their people. The victory made the Sasanians the equal of Rome and left its eastern frontier open to Persian raids.

In 296 or 297 the Sasanian king Narseh went to war with Rome and at first defeated the Caesar Galerius near Carrhae. In 298, however, Galerius surprised Narseh's camp at Satala in Armenia, capturing his treasury, wives and children, and then marched south to take the Persian capital Ctesiphon. To recover his family, Narseh accepted the terms agreed at Nisibis in 299. Persia handed over five provinces east of the Tigris, recognised the river as the border and gave up control of Iberia in the Caucasus. The frontier held for some forty years, and the Sasanian map shrank back from northern Mesopotamia and Armenia.

In 363 the Roman emperor Julian invaded Persia with a large army and a river fleet, aiming to take the Sasanian capital Ctesiphon and humble Shapur II. He advanced quickly down the Euphrates and won a battle outside Ctesiphon, but the city's defences looked too strong and his northern army never arrived. Julian burned his fleet and marched inland, where Shapur's scorched-earth tactics and constant raids forced a retreat, and Julian died of wounds from a skirmish near Samarra. His successor Jovian bought peace by handing Nisibis, Singara and other frontier lands to Persia and abandoning Armenia, regaining much of what Narseh had lost.

By the 5th century the Sasanians' greatest danger lay in the north-east, where the Hephthalites, a Hunnic people, had risen in Bactria in place of the Kidarites. Peroz I (459–484) had already been defeated and captured by them twice. Against the advice of his nobles and priests he launched a third campaign in 484; according to later accounts, the Hephthalite king Akhshunwar dug a hidden trench, and Peroz and much of his army fell into it and were killed. The Hephthalites seized Nishapur, Herat and Merv, and for years Persia paid them tribute, one of the lowest points in the empire's history.

Khosrow I (531–579) had made a 'Perpetual Peace' with the Byzantine emperor Justinian in 532, but angered by Byzantium's Arab clients, the Ghassanids, and urged on by envoys from Ostrogothic Italy, he broke it in 540. In May he invaded Byzantine Syria, sacking Sura and Beroea (Aleppo) and taking silver from towns that paid to be spared. In June he reached Antioch, the greatest city of the Roman East; when it refused to pay, he captured and sacked it. Khosrow resettled its captives in a new city near Ctesiphon called 'Khosrow's Better Antioch', and the raid showed that Persia could again strike deep into Roman lands.

In the 6th century Yemen, at the southern end of the Red Sea trade routes, was ruled by Ethiopians from the Christian kingdom of Aksum, allies of Byzantium. When an exiled Yemeni prince asked for help, Khosrow I sent the general Wahrez (Vahriz) by sea in about 570 with a small force; the sources give anything from 800 to 7,500 men. Wahrez killed the Aksumite ruler Masruq in battle, took San'a and restored a Himyarite king, Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan, as a Persian vassal. After a second invasion in the later 570s Yemen became a Sasanian province, stretching Persian power to the southern tip of Arabia.

The Byzantine emperor Maurice had helped Khosrow II regain his throne, so when Maurice was murdered by Phocas in 602, Khosrow declared war, ostensibly to avenge him. In 613 his general Shahrbaraz won victories at Antioch and Caesarea Maritima, and Jewish rebels, long persecuted under Byzantine rule, joined the advance; between 20,000 and 26,000 are said to have fought alongside the Persians. By mid-614 Jerusalem had fallen, after a siege of about three weeks according to one eyewitness account. The Persians carried the True Cross off to Ctesiphon, and with Palestine annexed, Persian rule now reached the Mediterranean coast.

After taking Syria and Palestine, Khosrow II's armies turned on Egypt, one of the Byzantine Empire's richest provinces. The invasion began in 617 or 618; the governor Nicetas, a cousin of Emperor Heraclius, could not resist and fled to Cyprus. According to the Khuzistan Chronicle, Alexandria was betrayed to the Persians in June 619, and by 621 they securely held the Nile valley. Egypt stayed in Persian hands for about ten years, ruled by Shahrbaraz from Alexandria. It was the first time the Sasanians had ruled Egypt, and with the Levant and parts of Anatolia also theirs, the empire was at its widest.

By 626 the Byzantine emperor Heraclius had been raiding deep into Persian territory for several years, so Khosrow II tried to end the war by striking at Constantinople itself. A Persian army under Shahrbaraz camped at Chalcedon, across the Bosphorus, while the Avars and their Slav allies, perhaps 80,000 strong, attacked the city's land walls from the European side from 29 June. The defenders under Patriarch Sergius and the patrician Bonus held the walls, and on 7 August Byzantine ships destroyed the rafts meant to ferry Persian troops across the strait. The siege collapsed, and its failure saved the Byzantine Empire from collapse.

Heraclius now carried the war into the heart of Persia. In September 627, allied with Turkic (Göktürk) troops who soon deserted him, he invaded Sasanian Mesopotamia in a risky winter campaign. On 12 December, near the ruins of ancient Nineveh, he met the Persian army of Rhahzadh; after about eight hours of fighting Rhahzadh was dead and his troops fell back. Heraclius plundered Khosrow II's palace at Dastagird, and soon afterwards the Persian army overthrew Khosrow and his son Kavad II sued for peace. The Sasanians gave up their conquests, the frontier returned roughly to where it had been around 590, and Persia slid into civil war.

Exhausted by the long Byzantine war and years of civil war, the Sasanians now faced the armies of the new Islamic state in Arabia, the Rashidun Caliphate. Caliph Umar sent Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas to Iraq with about 30,000 men, and from July 636 they faced a Persian army of perhaps 60,000, with war elephants, at al-Qadisiyyah, south of modern Kufa. In November 636, after several days of fighting, the Persian commander Rustam Farrokhzad was killed and his army collapsed. The defeat left the Sasanians unable to defend Mesopotamia and opened the road to their capital, Ctesiphon.

After al-Qadisiyyah the Arab army of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas advanced on Ctesiphon, the Persian capital on the Tigris since Parthian times. They besieged it from January to March 637, and when the defenders abandoned the city, King Yazdegerd III had already withdrawn to Hulwan in the Zagros foothills with much of the imperial treasure. Arab columns caught many of the refugees and seized huge booty. The fall of Ctesiphon consolidated Muslim rule over all of Mesopotamia, the empire's richest farmland, and confined the Sasanian state to the Iranian plateau.

Yazdegerd III still hoped to win back Mesopotamia, and gathered a large army in the Zagros Mountains. In 642 (some accounts say December 641) it met the Rashidun army of an-Nu'man ibn Muqarrin near Nahavand in western Iran. The battle was a catastrophic defeat for the Persians and marks the end of organised Sasanian resistance. Isfahan and other cities soon fell, and Yazdegerd escaped to the Merv region but could never raise another large army. The Iranian plateau now lay open, and over the following years the Arabs conquered it province by province.

After his defeats Yazdegerd III fled from province to province, through Kirman and Sakastan (Sistan) to Khorasan, hoping to raise new armies; he even asked Tang China for help, without success. He quarrelled with the local governors whose support he needed, and in 651, beaten once more, he took refuge with a miller near Merv. The miller murdered him, either for his jewels or, by another account, on the orders of the governor Mahoe Suri. His death ended the Sasanian dynasty after more than four centuries, and its lands passed to the caliphate, though Tabaristan by the Caspian held out for about a century.
